articles.title: Taylor Sheridan Accused of Stealing ‘Yellowstone’ From 2016 Pitch in Copyright Lawsuit
articles.summary: Writer Lauren J. Salkin has accused Taylor Sheridan of stealing his marquee series “Yellowstone” from her 2016 pitch in a lawsuit filed on Friday. 101 Studios, Paramount and Elevate Entertainment are also listed as defendants.
body: Reps for Sheridan, 101 Studios, Paramount and Elevate Entertainment did not immediately respond to Variety ’s request for comment.

The lawsuit lists several “specific expressive choices” that “Yellowstone” allegedly lifted from Salkin’s “Sovereign Nation.” Those elements, the suit states, include “a tribal casino functioning as the institutional center of political and development power; a signature confrontation staged in the tribal chairman’s casino office over expansion beyond reservation boundaries; the use of trust land, the absence of zoning restrictions, and a 99-year lease structure as the concrete mechanism for that expansion; and recurring master-plan imagery deployed to dramatize the struggle for territorial control.”

Salkin’s lawyers also claim that she “proposed” Danny Huston and Gil Birmingham for “Sovereign Nation” in her pitch deck. Both were later cast in “Yellowstone” and played “materially parallel structural roles: Birmingham as the tribal political leader whose authority and development strategy run through the casino, and Huston as the outside development power broker who supplies the political or commercial path for that expansion.”

articles.title: Mark Ruffalo Fires Back After Paramount Slammed His Merger Attack as ‘Antisemitic’: ‘Appalling and Fundamentally Dishonest’
articles.summary: Mark Ruffalo has fired back at Paramount after the company slammed the actor as “antisemitic” for accusing David and Larry Ellison of “powering some of the most destructive and inhuman forces in the world.” “The accusation that I am antisemitic is appalling and fundamentally dishonest,” Ruffalo…
body: “This merger has real consequences for real people, and for the entire country,” Ruffalo added. “Scrutinizing the Ellisons, including Oracle’s business built on data, surveillance technology and government contracts, and the serious threat to editorial freedom and the loss of a livelihood for thousands of families, is fair and necessary. The $111 billion deal would hand one family control over CNN, HBO and Warner Bros., backed in part by foreign money whose influence on editorial decisions has never been fully explained to the public.”

After Ruffalo’s initial post, a spokesperson for Paramount said in a statement that the company is “troubled when antisemitic tropes are invoked in purported service of a business dispute. Words like ‘genocide’ and ‘apartheid,’ applied to a corporate transaction, aren’t just wrong — they’re a bridge too far, and they cheapen the very real suffering those words are meant to describe. This doesn’t deserve a response in kind — and to be clear, we don’t tolerate prejudice of any kind, against anyone.”

articles.title: Why Do We Love Spider-Man So Much?
articles.summary: Why does everyone love Spider-Man so much? When “Spider-Man: No Way Home” came out at the end of 2021, it made an insane amount of money ($814 million in the U.S. alone), blasting away any vestige of that era’s comic-book-movie fatigue.
body: But “ Spider-Man: Brand New Day ” has rewritten the playbook again. The movie is a solid and well-executed adventure, no more and no less, in which Holland’s Peter Parker and his love, MJ (Zendaya), barely even get to talk (because she doesn’t remember who she is). No one is pretending that “Brand New Day” is as great as, say, “Spider-Man 2.” Yet despite that, it is now likely to become… the top-grossing movie of all time. At least until the next Spider-Man adventure comes along.

Why Spider-Man, why now? Ever since his debut in 1962, he has been immensely popular (though Stan Lee had to fight a skeptical publisher to approve the character). But if you look back over 50 years of American comic-book-movie culture, it’s undeniable that the two reigning superheroes have been Superman and Batman. Christopher Reeve’s performance in the first two “Superman” films remains, to me (and many others), the most perfect live-action embodiment of a superhero there has ever been. Those first two films loom mythologically.

articles.title: ‘Embryonic’: lost novel by French film-maker Éric Rohmer is republished
articles.summary: English translation of Élisabeth, the New Wave director’s 1946 book about young lovers in prewar Paris, receives rave reviews as precursor to auteur’s cinematic work. In the dog days of the second world war, 24-year-old Maurice Schérer wrote a tale of young lovers in prewar small-town France.
body: Now – eight decades on from its first publication, 16 years on from its author’s death – Élisabeth belatedly returns from the cold. Republished in an English-language translation by Aaron Kerner, Rohmer’s book has been greeted with glowing reviews, hailed as a lost modernist classic and a crucial origin story for the award-winning director of Claire’s Knee, The Green Ray and My Night at Maud’s. “It would be a rewarding, exciting read even if the identity of its author were unfamiliar,” wrote Richard Brody in the New Yorker. The fact that it’s by Rohmer? That’s the icing on the cake.

“On the one hand, to be honest, the book is a footnote,” says the novelist André Aciman, a longtime Rohmer fan who wrote the foreword to the new edition. “But it is also embryonic and full of Rohmerian moments. It takes on all the themes that will become more developed, complex and impactful in his films.”

articles.title: Nigel Havers: ‘My biggest disappointment? Not playing James Bond’
articles.summary: The actor on mucking out pigs as a teenager, an apology to his first wife and what makes him cry all the time. Born in London, Nigel Havers, 74, was Bafta-nominated for his 1981 role in Chariots of Fire. His other films include A Passage to India and Empire of the Sun.
body: What is your greatest fear? Every actor has the same fear – ie, you’re never going to work again.
What is your earliest memory? Being in a pram in London and there being a road accident ahead and saying to my mother, “Go quickly, I want to see what’s happened.”
Which living person do you most admire, and why? The king – because he’s been through quite a bit and I think he’s come out the other side brilliantly.
What is the trait you most deplore in others? When they don’t tell the truth.

articles.title: Stand By Me at 40: Rob Reiner’s seminal coming-of-age saga remains a bittersweet triumph
articles.summary: The late director’s sensitive and detailed adaptation of Stephen King’s novella has an authenticity that so many imitators could never replicate. Coming-of-age metaphors don’t get any blunter than a group of preteen boys following a set of railroad tracks to a classmate’s dead body, a sobering…
body: Though set a few years earlier than American Graffiti, Stand By Me feels like a natural companion to it, another radio-friendly nostalgia piece about a transitional moment for male friends in small-town America. Both films are death-haunted but the difference is that the characters in American Graffiti, who are reaching young adulthood at the cusp of the Vietnam war, don’t know what the future holds and writer-director George Lucas saves that bummer news for the epilogue. The boys in Reiner’s film know what lies at the end of a 20- to 30-mile hike down the tracks and their attraction to the novelty and notoriety of seeing a dead peer turns morbid. Their steps grow heavier by the hour.
points: The late director’s sensitive and detailed adaptation of Stephen King’s novella has an authenticity that so many imitators could never replicate.

articles.title: Before ‘The Pitt,’ There Was ‘St. Elsewhere’
articles.summary: The Emmy-winning NBC medical drama that launched the careers of Denzel Washington and Mark Harmon ended by suggesting its entire six-season run existed inside the imagination of an autistic child — a twist that remains one of television’s most debated endings.
body: Though it was never an outright hit, St. Elsewhere punched way above its weight in terms of the careers it helped launch and a style that set the template for medical dramas that followed it. The show can also boast one of the more memorable series finales in TV history.

When the series debuted, that style was seen as a barrier to success: Reviewing the show in November 1982, THR critic Richard Hack wrote, “So real and graphic is the drama being presented here that we cannot believe that 20 million people across this country will find it entertaining enough to flip to.”

Nonetheless, St. Elsewhere would win 13 Emmys over its run, including six for its fourth season in 1986. It was nominated for best drama series in all six seasons, though it never took home that honor.

Three of the show’s regulars — William Daniels, Bonnie Bartlett and Ed Flanders — won acting Emmys for their roles. Equally impressive was the show’s eye for emerging talent: It helped kick-start the careers of Denzel Washington, Mark Harmon and David Morse, as well as comedian Howie Mandel, playing against type in a dramatic role.

articles.title: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Swinging to Fourth Box Office Victory as It Tops ‘Insidious’ Sequel
articles.summary: Tom Holland's superhero blockbuster continues its dominance against the launches of 'Insidious: Out of the Further' and Jason Statham's 'Mutiny.'
body: Spider-Man: Brand New Day continues to deliver in its fourth weekend at the box office as it faces off against newcomers Insidious: Out of the Further and the Jason Statham -led Mutiny.

Insidious: Out of the Further occupies second place with $10.6 million on Friday, including Thursday previews. Sony projects an opening weekend of $23.7 million for the sixth installment in the horror franchise that hails from Screen Gems, Stage 6 Films and Blumhouse Atomic Monster and kicked off with 2011’s original Insidious. Out of the Further earned a C+ CinemaScore, tying 2023’s Insidious: The Red Door for the series’ lowest grade.

Debuting in 3,330 North American theaters, Out of the Further stars Amelia Eve, Brandon Perea and Lin Shaye and centers on a young mother who can bring spirits back with her to the real world. It follows The Red Door, which saw the return of original series stars Patrick Wilson and Rose Byrne. That one opened to an impressive $33 million domestically before grossing $189 million worldwide throughout its run.
points: Tom Holland's superhero blockbuster continues its dominance against the launches of 'Insidious: Out of the Further' and Jason Statham's 'Mutiny.'

articles.title: Out Of The Further Proves One Thing About The Insidious Franchise
articles.summary: While Insidious: Out of the Further is the sixth movie in the Insidious franchise, it's also proof of the horror property's potential longevity.
body: Where we go after we die, if we go anywhere at all, is the true root of all religions. Sure, finding community through a shared moral standard is what keeps many practicing, but the desire to make sense of mortality and the refusal to accept death as the true end motivated early humans to conceptualize ideas of the Afterlife, souls, continued existence through reincarnation, and ghosts. There will never be any definitive, evidence-based "proof" of an Afterlife, but it sure is fun to think about.

Personally, I hope that James Wan and Leigh Whannell are right, and that the Further — the ghostly dimension where souls are damned to remain forever — is the flavor of purgatory that actually exists. Established in the original "Insidious" movie in 2010, the Further is a dark dimension which was never meant to be seen or experienced by the living. Yet, like the endless labyrinth shown in Kane Parsons' "Backrooms," parts of the Further resemble the material dimension and can replicate environments pulled from memories.
